text: Every day, millions of people recite the Quran.
They know its sound by heart.
But for most of them, the meaning stays behind a translation.
What if you could understand it directly, word by word, in the language it was revealed in?
This is Quranki.
Here's the surprising part.
The Quran has seventy-seven thousand words, but they come from fewer than five thousand dictionary forms.
And they're not spread evenly.
Just ten words make up a quarter of the whole text.
The top one hundred cover more than half.
Learn about five hundred, and you'll recognize eighty percent of every page.
So Quranki teaches words in the order the Quran actually uses them.
It schedules every review with FSRS, the algorithm behind modern Anki.
And it brings each word straight back to the ayahs where it appears.
It runs on the web, on iPhone, and on Android, and your progress syncs between them.
Let's look at a real account, about eleven weeks in.
This is the Learn page.
Today there are forty-four words waiting: thirty reviews and fourteen new words.
Eight hundred forty-eight words mastered, a fifty-two day streak, and about fifteen minutes of study a day.
The curriculum moves in stages, from the most frequent words to the ninety-nine names of Allah.
Start a session and you see the Arabic first.
Try to recall the meaning, then reveal it.
Every word comes with an ayah where it really appears, glossed word by word, so you learn it in context.
Then rate yourself: again, hard, good, or easy.
Each button tells you exactly when you'll see the word next.
On desktop, it's all keyboard driven.
Now the best part.
Open any surah in the reader.
Words you've learned appear without a translation, because you already know them.
Only new words keep their gloss, and every ayah shows how much of it you understand.
Forget a word?
Click it for a quick hint.
Want the full meaning?
Open the translation.
Right-click any word for its grammar, lemma, and root, and how often it appears in the Quran.
Understanding leads naturally to memorizing.
Once you know seventy percent of a ruku's words, it unlocks in Memorize.
You see the opening words, recite the rest from memory, then check yourself.
The same scheduler decides when it's time to revise.
Progress shows the big picture.
This learner now recognizes eighty-one percent of the words in the Quran.
You can see how well they follow a typical ayah, and every surah gets its own bar.
On desktop there is a command palette, so you can jump to any ayah, like two two fifty-five, in a keystroke.
Pin your place, collect ayahs into bookmarks, and read in dark or light.
And it all comes with you.
On iPhone, the same account picks up right where you left off.
The same reviews, each word inside its ayah.
The same reader, with a hint on tap and full details on a long press.
Your ruku revision for the day, and every statistic in your pocket.
Quranki also publishes free guides built on real corpus data: the most common words, how many you need, how long it takes, and why spaced repetition makes them stick.
Quranki.
Learn the words, read the Quran, and understand it.
Start free at quranki dot org, or download it on iPhone and Android.
